objections.objection: The draft cites the Heudel scoping review as volume 11 of its journal; multiple independent sources cite it as volume 12.
objections.quote: Heudel PE, Crochet H, Filori Q, Bachelot T, Blay JY. Artificial intelligence in medicine: a scoping review of the risk of deskilling and loss of expertise among physicians. ESMO Real World Data and Digital Oncology 2026;11(C):100693
objections.why: The paper's DOI resolves to the ESMO journal's own page, and a citing paper in Advances in Respiratory Medicine gives the volume as 12, not 11. A wrong volume number in a source citation is a verifiable factual error that a reader checking the reference would immediately find.

objections.objection: The draft says 'Nothing false was printed' about Fortune's coverage, but Fortune's article mischaracterises the study design by saying the drop occurred after the AI was taken away, when the study actually measured performance during AI use on the days without it.
objections.quote: Nothing false was printed. The number simply arrived in its most alarming accurate form, with none of the reasons to hold it loosely.
objections.why: Fortune's article states the drop happened 'after they no longer had access to the AI tools they were introduced to.' The study measured non-AI performance during a period when AI was in use on other days — not after removal. The draft itself makes this design distinction central to its entire analysis of the Norwegian study. Saying 'nothing false was printed' about an article that gets the study design wrong contradicts the draft's own framework and is factually incorrect.
objections.fix: Replace 'Nothing false was printed' with something like: 'The number was accurate; the study design was not — Fortune described the drop as occurring after the AI was taken away, when the study measured performance during AI use, on the days without it.'

objections.objection: The draft says the Heudel review's abstract calls the colonoscopy study 'a multicenter randomized trial' but does not note that the same abstract sentence also mischaracterises the study design a second way, saying the drop occurred 'when endoscopists reverted to non-AI procedures after repeated AI use' — implying the AI had been removed, which it had not.
objections.quote: Its abstract describes the colonoscopy study as 'a multicenter randomized trial'; the study is retrospective and observational, as the review's own body says.
objections.why: The draft correctly flags the 'randomized trial' error. The same sentence in the Heudel abstract contains a second error — 'reverted to non-AI procedures after repeated AI use' implies the AI was withdrawn, whereas the endoscopists were still using it on other days. Reporting one error in a sentence and missing a second in the same sentence means the full extent of the abstract's inaccuracy is understated. This is the same design distinction the draft treats as the most important finding in the Norwegian section.
objections.fix: After noting the 'multicenter randomized trial' error, add: 'The same sentence also says the drop occurred when endoscopists reverted to non-AI procedures after repeated AI use, implying the AI had been removed; in fact they were still using it on other days during the same period.'

objections.objection: The draft characterises the Heudel review as a 'scoping review' throughout, but the review's own abstract describes the method as 'a narrative review'; the paper's title says 'scoping review' while its methods say 'narrative review', and the draft does not note this internal inconsistency in the paper it is criticising for internal inconsistencies.
objections.quote: Heudel and colleagues at the Centre Léon Bérard published a scoping review of exactly this question in 2026.
objections.why: The draft's label matches the paper's title, so it is not wrong. But the draft spends considerable space documenting internal inconsistencies in the Heudel review — abstract vs body on the 7%/30% figure, abstract vs body on the study design — and does not note that the paper's own title ('scoping review') conflicts with its abstract's method description ('narrative review'). A page that checks other people's arithmetic should show its own, as the draft itself says.
objections.fix: Add a parenthetical noting that the paper's title says 'scoping review' while its abstract describes the method as 'a narrative review', and that this page uses the title's term.

inferences.quote: the senior author of the deskilling study is a co-author of the prospective study that found none
inferences.problem: Yuichi Mori is the last-listed author of the Budzyń study, which in many journals signals senior authorship, but the draft asserts this as fact without noting that first authorship (Budzyń) and corresponding authorship (Romańczyk) are the roles the paper itself designates; calling Mori 'the senior author' is an inference about internal credit that the author list alone does not settle unambiguously.
inferences.correct_reading: Yuichi Mori is the last-listed author of the Budzyń study and a co-author of the Pedersen study; the ASCO Post identifies him as senior author, which is consistent with last-author convention, so the claim is defensible but rests on convention rather than explicit designation in the paper.
inferences.fix: Yuichi Mori — last-listed author of the deskilling study and a co-author of the prospective study that found none.

inferences.quote: A fact-check run on this page reported that this letter mis-describes the study's design in its opening sentence. That would be a second instance of the error this page is about, in the same journal as the study — and we are not printing it as a finding, because we could not open the letter to read the sentence ourselves.
inferences.problem: The abstract of the Levartovsky and Kopylov letter is publicly visible at the Lancet's own abstract page and states the study showed a decline 'after computer-aided detection introduction and subsequent removal' — but the Budzyń study measured performance during AI exposure (on non-AI days), not after removal. The draft treats the letter as unread when its abstract, which contains the sentence in question, is accessible without a subscription and was returned by a standard search.
inferences.correct_reading: The letter's abstract is publicly accessible and confirms the mischaracterisation the fact-check identified: it describes the Budzyń finding as a decline 'after computer-aided detection introduction and subsequent removal,' whereas the study measured performance during AI exposure on non-AI days — not after the tool was withdrawn. The draft can and should report this, with the caveat that only the abstract, not the full letter, was read.
inferences.fix: A fact-check run on this page reported that this letter mis-describes the study's design in its opening sentence. The letter's abstract — which is publicly accessible — describes the finding as a decline 'after computer-aided detection introduction and subsequent removal'; the Budzyń study measured performance during AI exposure, on non-AI days, not after the tool was withdrawn. We have read the abstract but not the full letter, and report the abstract's opening characterisation accordingly.

inferences.quote: the total number of procedures in the second period nearly doubled, from 795 to 1,382 — while the non-AI procedures actually measured fell from 795 to 648
inferences.problem: This is arithmetically correct and clearly explained, but the juxtaposition could mislead a reader into thinking the 1,382 figure is the comparator for the 795 non-AI procedures. The draft handles this well in context, but the sentence in isolation implies the measured group shrank while the total grew, without making explicit that the 1,382 includes AI-assisted procedures that were not part of the comparison.
inferences.correct_reading: The 795 pre-period procedures were all non-AI (AI did not yet exist in those centres); the 1,382 post-period procedures included both AI-assisted and non-AI colonoscopies, of which 648 were non-AI and thus measured. The shrinkage of the measured group and the growth of the total are both real and both explained correctly in the surrounding text.
inferences.fix: the total number of procedures in the second period nearly doubled, from 795 to 1,382 — of which 648 were non-AI-assisted and thus measured, down from 795 before AI was introduced

inferences.quote: doctors became 20% worse at spotting abnormalities on their own
inferences.problem: The draft attributes this phrasing to Fortune's headline and correctly notes that 'about a fifth is the relative one, and both are true.' However, the draft's own framing — 'Six points is the absolute fall and about a fifth is the relative one' — slightly mischaracterises the relative calculation: 6.0 percentage points divided by 28.4% is approximately 21.1%, not exactly 'about a fifth' (20%). This is a rounding issue, not a fabrication, but the draft is presenting itself as a precision check.
inferences.correct_reading: The relative reduction is 6.0/28.4 = approximately 21%, which Fortune rounds to 20%. Both the absolute (6 percentage points) and relative (~21%) figures are derivable from the data; the draft's 'about a fifth' is a reasonable approximation.
inferences.fix: Six points is the absolute fall and about a fifth — more precisely, 21% — is the relative one

inferences.quote: finding no deskilling after the tool is withdrawn is consistent with an effect that faded, and equally consistent with one that was never there
inferences.problem: This is a sound inferential statement about the Norwegian study's null result, but the draft does not apply the same logic symmetrically: it does not note that the Polish result (a fall during AI exposure) is equally consistent with a confound (the population change) as with a genuine deskilling effect. The asymmetry — scepticism applied to the null but not equally to the positive finding — is a calibration issue, not a factual error, and the draft does acknowledge the Polish study's confounders elsewhere.
inferences.correct_reading: Both studies are observational and both results are consistent with multiple explanations. The draft correctly applies this logic to the Norwegian null but does not restate it symmetrically when summarising the Polish positive finding in the same paragraph.
inferences.fix: finding no deskilling after the tool is withdrawn is consistent with an effect that faded, and equally consistent with one that was never there — just as the Polish fall is consistent with genuine deskilling and equally consistent with the population change the authors themselves list as their largest limitation

inferences.quote: the absence of a fall argues against the idea that exposure to CADe erodes skills, at least for nonexperienced endoscopists, although such skill reduction has been observed in another study involving only experienced endoscopists — and the study they cite there is the Polish one
inferences.problem: The draft quotes this as the Norwegian authors' discussion being 'narrower than their stated conclusion, which covers all experience levels.' But the Norwegian authors' stated conclusion ('no upskilling or deskilling was observed') does cover all experience levels, while their discussion qualifies it to inexperienced endoscopists. The draft correctly identifies this tension but then attributes the narrower claim to the discussion without flagging that the abstract-level conclusion is broader — which is itself an instance of the abstract/body discrepancy the draft criticises in the scoping review.
inferences.correct_reading: The Norwegian paper's abstract-level conclusion covers all experience levels; its discussion narrows the deskilling inference to inexperienced endoscopists. This is the same abstract/body discrepancy the draft criticises in the scoping review, and the draft should note the parallel rather than only attributing the narrower reading to the discussion.
inferences.fix: Add a parenthetical: '(the Norwegian paper's abstract states no effect at any experience level, while its discussion narrows the deskilling inference to inexperienced endoscopists — the same abstract/body gap this page identifies in the scoping review)'

inferences.quote: A group that did not visibly gain from the tool is weak evidence about what losing the tool does to them.
inferences.problem: This is a sound inferential point, but it is stated as a conclusion rather than as one reading of the data. The experienced group's null result during AI use is also consistent with a ceiling effect (already high performers) or with the algorithm-aversion the authors themselves name — neither of which implies the group is uninformative about deskilling. The draft's phrasing implies the experienced group's data are simply uninformative, when the authors offer a specific mechanistic explanation for why they did not engage with the tool.
inferences.correct_reading: The experienced group's failure to gain from the tool is explained by the authors as possible algorithm aversion, not merely as absence of engagement. A group that did not use the tool as intended is indeed weak evidence about what losing it does to them, but the reason matters: aversion is different from indifference, and the distinction affects what the null implies.
inferences.fix: A group that the authors suggest may have actively avoided the tool — through algorithm aversion — is weak evidence about what losing the tool does to them.

inferences.quote: Its outcome measures are scoring error against a consensus standard and agreement between readers, not sensitivity or reading time.
inferences.problem: The draft correctly identifies that the scoping review's summary of the Savardi paper is wrong (32 residents, sensitivity, reading time, three-month follow-up — none of which appear in the paper). This finding is sound and well-supported. No error here — flagging as confirmed correct for completeness.
inferences.correct_reading: Confirmed correct: the Savardi paper has eight radiologists, uses intraclass correlation and scoring error as outcomes, and has no follow-up. The scoping review's summary is wrong on all four counts the draft identifies.

inferences.quote: The experienced group is where care is needed. It shows no significant effect in any phase — but that includes no benefit while the AI was running
inferences.problem: The draft uses the experienced group's null-during-AI result to cast doubt on what the null-after-AI result means for them. This is a legitimate inferential point. However, the draft does not note that the experienced group's null-during-AI result is itself consistent with the Norwegian authors' explanation (algorithm aversion leading to non-use), which would mean the tool was not actually tested in that group — making the post-withdrawal null even less informative than the draft implies.
inferences.correct_reading: If experienced endoscopists largely did not use the tool (as the authors suggest), then neither the during-AI nor the after-AI result for that group tests the deskilling hypothesis. The draft's inference is correct in direction but understates how uninformative the experienced group's data are.
inferences.fix: The experienced group is where care is needed. It shows no significant effect in any phase — but that includes no benefit while the AI was running, and the authors suggest this may reflect algorithm aversion rather than genuine engagement with the tool, which would make the post-withdrawal null for this group even less informative about deskilling.

inferences.quote: We give the number that its own flow diagram supports: 65 assessed, 53 excluded with reasons, 12 included. The earlier steps of that diagram do not reconcile — 432 database records and 41 from grey literature, less 37 duplicates, is 436 rather than the 373 printed, and 373 less 332 excluded is 41 rather than the 65 it then reports assessing.
inferences.problem: The arithmetic the draft presents as its own check is correct and the discrepancies are real. However, the draft does not consider the possibility that the PRISMA flow diagram uses a different deduplication step or that some records were excluded before screening in a way not shown — which is a common source of apparent PRISMA arithmetic errors. The draft presents the discrepancy as an error in the review without acknowledging that PRISMA flows sometimes have legitimate intermediate steps not shown in the diagram.
inferences.correct_reading: The arithmetic discrepancies in the flow diagram are real as stated. They may reflect an error in the review, or they may reflect intermediate steps not shown in the diagram. The draft should note both possibilities rather than presenting the discrepancy as a confirmed error.
inferences.fix: The earlier steps of that diagram do not reconcile — 432 database records and 41 from grey literature, less 37 duplicates, is 436 rather than the 373 printed, and 373 less 332 excluded is 41 rather than the 65 it then reports assessing. This may reflect an error in the diagram or intermediate steps not shown; we cannot determine which from the published PDF.

inferences.quote: its abstract describes the colonoscopy study as 'a multicenter randomized trial'
inferences.problem: This is a confirmed factual error in the scoping review, correctly identified by the draft. The Budzyń study is explicitly described as a retrospective observational study in its own title and abstract. The draft's identification of this error is sound and well-supported.
inferences.correct_reading: Confirmed correct: the Budzyń study is a retrospective observational study; the scoping review's abstract calling it a randomised trial is wrong. No change needed to the draft's handling of this.

inferences.quote: over 30% of participants reversed correct initial diagnoses in a pathology experiment under time pressure, where its body puts the same study at 7% of judgments
inferences.problem: The draft correctly identifies that the scoping review's abstract (>30%) and body (7%) report different figures for the same study, and correctly notes 'both figures can be true of one dataset — they have different denominators.' However, the draft does not specify what the two denominators are, leaving the reader unable to evaluate whether the abstract figure is misleading or merely uses a different base. The draft should either specify the denominators or acknowledge it cannot, rather than leaving the reconciliation implicit.
inferences.correct_reading: The 7% figure (from the Rosbach paper) is the share of initially correct judgments overturned by erroneous AI advice. The >30% figure in the scoping review's abstract likely uses a different denominator — possibly all judgments, or all cases where the AI was wrong. The draft correctly flags the discrepancy but should note it cannot verify the abstract's denominator without access to the review's calculation.
inferences.fix: Its abstract also reports that over 30% of participants reversed correct initial diagnoses in a pathology experiment under time pressure, where its body puts the same study at 7% of judgments overturned by erroneous AI advice. Both figures can be true of one dataset with different denominators — the 7% is the share of initially correct judgments overturned; we cannot verify what denominator the abstract's figure uses.

inferences.quote: This is not a study about skills decaying over months. It is a study about what happens inside a single reading, and it is the clearest measurement in this entire field of the thing people actually describe when they say AI has changed how they work: you take what it gives you.
inferences.problem: The claim that the Dratsch mammography automation-bias study is 'the clearest measurement in this entire field' of the described phenomenon is an evaluative superlative that the draft does not support with a comparison across all studies in the field. The scoping review includes twelve studies; the draft has not read all of them at source and cannot rank them on this dimension.
inferences.correct_reading: The Dratsch study is a clear and well-designed measurement of automation bias in a single reading session. Whether it is the clearest in the field depends on studies the draft has not read at source.
inferences.fix: This is not a study about skills decaying over months. It is a study about what happens inside a single reading, and it is among the clearest measurements in this literature of the thing people actually describe when they say AI has changed how they work: you take what it gives you.

inferences.quote: Three randomised experiments — 1,222 people randomised, 1,060 analysed — had participants work through practice problems with or without AI, then removed the AI without warning and gave them three more. Unassisted solve rates fell, at effect sizes of −0.42, −0.19 and −0.42, and people gave up sooner. That is causal
inferences.problem: Calling the result 'causal' is warranted by the randomised design, but the draft immediately qualifies it as 'about fifteen minutes long' and 'a preprint with no pre-registration statement.' The word 'causal' without those qualifications in the same sentence will be the part a reader quotes. The causal claim is for the specific fifteen-minute task context, not for skill decay in general, and the draft's own framing ('which is internal replication by one team in one preprint') should be in the same sentence as 'causal.'
inferences.correct_reading: The randomised design supports a causal inference that AI access during a short practice session reduced unassisted performance immediately after — in a fifteen-minute task, in a preprint, by one team. The word 'causal' is technically correct but will be read as stronger than the evidence carries without the qualifications in the same sentence.
inferences.fix: Unassisted solve rates fell, at effect sizes of −0.42, −0.19 and −0.42, and people gave up sooner. That is a causal finding — for a fifteen-minute task, in a single preprint, by one team — and it held in all three experiments.

inferences.quote: participants consulted it on more than half of trials and, having consulted it, followed it on 79.8% of the trials where it was wrong
inferences.problem: The draft correctly reports this figure from the Shaw and Nave working paper. However, it does not note that 'followed it' on trials where it was wrong is not the same as 'was wrong because of it' — participants may have independently reached the same wrong answer. The 79.8% figure measures agreement with wrong AI answers, not the causal share of errors attributable to the AI.
inferences.correct_reading: 79.8% of chat-engaged trials where the AI was wrong resulted in the participant giving the same wrong answer. This measures agreement, not causation — some participants may have independently reached the wrong answer. The figure is still striking but should not be read as 'the AI caused 79.8% of errors on those trials.'
inferences.fix: having consulted it, gave the same wrong answer on 79.8% of the trials where it was wrong

inferences.quote: The most-cited meta-analysis finding that ChatGPT improves learning — cited several hundred times — its own journal's counter read 402 at one point on 30 August 2026 and 399 an hour later, which is what live metrics do, and other counts of the same paper run from 262 to over 500 — was retracted by its journal on 22 April 2026.
inferences.problem: The parenthetical about citation counts fluctuating is accurate and appropriately hedged. No inferential error here. The retraction date and ground are attributed to the retraction notice, which the draft lists as a source. This is sound.
inferences.correct_reading: No error. The draft correctly reports the retraction and appropriately hedges the citation count.

inferences.quote: Stanković and colleagues close their comment with a judgement of that one paper and not of the field — they are describing the study they audited, and this page carries it as their verdict on it rather than as a finding about the field.
inferences.problem: This is a correct and important qualification. The draft handles it well. No error.

inferences.quote: The Norwegian endoscopists had it taken away entirely.
inferences.problem: This is accurate as a description of phase 3 of the Pedersen study, but the draft does not note that two of the thirteen Norwegian endoscopists ran CADe throughout the entire study (including during the withdrawal phase), as the paper itself states. The draft mentions this detail later ('two endoscopists ran it throughout while the rest switched it on only during withdrawal') but not at the point where it draws the contrast with the Polish study, which is where a reader will form their impression of the design difference.
inferences.correct_reading: Most Norwegian endoscopists had CADe removed in phase 3, but two ran it throughout. The contrast with the Polish study is real but slightly overstated at the point where it is drawn.
inferences.fix: Most Norwegian endoscopists had it taken away entirely in phase 3 (two ran it throughout).

inferences.quote: On 5 June 2026, two days after the Norwegian trial appeared, Gastroenterology published an editorial by Weinberg and Bretthauer titled Upskilling, Deskilling, or Never Skilling: Who Benefits From Artificial Intelligence in Colonoscopy? Michael Bretthauer is an author of the Polish deskilling study.
inferences.problem: The draft says the editorial was published 'two days after the Norwegian trial appeared' (3 June 2026). PubMed records the editorial as published online 5 June 2026. The Norwegian trial was published online 3 June 2026. The two-day gap is correct. However, the draft implies the editorial was responding to the Norwegian trial, when the editorial may have been written and accepted before the Norwegian trial appeared — the two-day gap is too short for a response editorial to be written, reviewed, and published. The draft should not imply a causal or responsive relationship it cannot establish.
inferences.correct_reading: The editorial appeared two days after the Norwegian trial online, but the timeline is too compressed for the editorial to have been written in response to it. Both likely appeared in the same publication cycle. The draft should not imply the editorial was prompted by the Norwegian trial.
inferences.fix: On 5 June 2026, the same week the Norwegian trial appeared online, Gastroenterology published an editorial by Weinberg and Bretthauer titled Upskilling, Deskilling, or Never Skilling: Who Benefits From Artificial Intelligence in Colonoscopy?

best_coverage.got_right: Carried the SMC volume-confounder caveat by name, quoting Osmani's point that the total number of colonoscopies increased and that increased workload could have led to fatigue and poorer detection. Also quoted Tucker on automation bias not being unique to AI. Correctly framed the study as observational throughout. Preserved both the absolute and relative framings of the result.
best_coverage.still_omitted: Did not name the Polish screening-programme suspension as the specific mechanism behind the volume doubling, did not mention withdrawal-time data being absent, did not note the eleven limitations as a count, and did not flag that the study was retrospective in a way that would alert a lay reader to what that forecloses causally.

best_coverage.got_right: Reported both the 20% relative and 6% absolute reduction correctly. Quoted the authors acknowledging the observational nature and that factors other than AI may have influenced findings. Quoted senior author Mori raising the implication for prior RCTs. Quoted the companion UCL commentary with appropriate hedging language. Noted limited generalisability to less experienced endoscopists and called for further studies.
best_coverage.still_omitted: Did not name the Polish screening-programme suspension or quantify the volume doubling (795 to 1,382 total procedures). Did not mention withdrawal-time data being absent, blinding, or the exclusion of the first 100 procedures per centre. Did not report the confidence interval or P-value.

best_coverage.outlet: American College of Gastroenterology Evidence-Based GI (Zhou), September 2025
best_coverage.got_right: Explicitly flagged observational design susceptible to confounding and selection bias. Noted residual confounding despite multivariable adjustment. Flagged insufficient colonoscopies per endoscopist to allow per-operator analysis. Cited Troya et al. (the eye-tracking paper) as a proposed mechanism. Correctly labelled the study as observational throughout.
best_coverage.still_omitted: The draft notes it missed the mechanism paragraph on first read (its own disclosed error). The publicly accessible text does not appear to name the Polish screening-programme suspension as the specific driver of the volume change, nor does it report the confidence interval. The draft also notes it could not access the companion commentary published in the same journal issue.

best_coverage.got_right: Correctly described the study as 'a large observational study.' Reported both the 20% relative and 6% absolute reduction in the same sentence, preserving both framings without choosing the more alarming one exclusively. Reported the AI-assisted ADR (25.3%) alongside the non-AI figures, giving readers the full comparison. Noted that the number of adenomas per colonoscopy and advanced adenomas per colonoscopy did not change significantly between periods — a finding the draft does not mention and which is relevant to the severity question.
best_coverage.still_omitted: No mention of the volume doubling or its cause, no confidence interval, no withdrawal-time limitation, no call for prospective trials, no mention of the eleven limitations as a body.

best_coverage.got_right: Correctly labelled the study as a 'retrospective observational study' in the body text. Noted that multivariable logistic regression was used to control for confounders including patient age, sex, sedation, bowel prep, and endoscopist characteristics. Quoted an external expert (ASGE chair Prateek Sharma) contextualising the result against the broader AI-in-colonoscopy literature. Fact-checked by a named PhD.
best_coverage.still_omitted: Did not name the Polish screening-programme suspension or quantify the volume doubling. Did not report the confidence interval. Did not mention withdrawal-time data being absent or the exclusion of the first 100 procedures per centre.

best_coverage.outlet: Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology research highlight (Ray), September 5 2025
best_coverage.got_right: Correctly labelled the study as 'a new multicentre, observational study' and 'retrospective study' in its own text. Correctly reported the n=795 before and n=648 after figures for non-AI-assisted colonoscopies. Did not misrepresent the study design as randomised.
best_coverage.still_omitted: No limitations stated, no confidence interval, no mention of the volume doubling or its cause, no expert quotes, no call for prospective trials. The draft's characterisation of this piece as reporting 'figures as fact with no limitations and no quotes' is accurate for the limitations and quotes, but the design label is correct — it is not a case of misrepresenting the study as randomised.

contradictions.quote: A research highlight in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology reported the figures as fact with no limitations and no quotes.
contradictions.counterexample: Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology (Ray, September 2025) correctly labelled the study as 'a new multicentre, observational study' and 'retrospective study' in its own text, and accurately reported the n=795/n=648 split. It did not misrepresent the design. The draft's complaint that it carried 'no limitations and no quotes' is accurate, but the implicit suggestion that it misrepresented the study type is not supported.
contradictions.fix: Narrow the claim: 'A research highlight in Nature Reviews Gastroenterology & Hepatology correctly labelled the study as retrospective and observational, but reported the figures without limitations, without expert quotes, and without naming the volume confounder.'

contradictions.quote: Fortune carried the six-point fall to a business readership on 26 August 2025, connected it to an automation analogy and to a Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon study, and reported none of the eleven limitations.
contradictions.counterexample: This is accurate as far as it goes for Fortune itself. However, the draft uses Fortune as its lead instance of the general failure of caveats to travel, immediately after saying 'none of it crossed the boundary.' Time.com — a comparable general-audience outlet — did carry the volume-confounder caveat by name on the same day the study published, citing Osmani's SMC comment directly. The claim that caveats did not cross the boundary to general-audience coverage is therefore overstated: at least one major general outlet carried the key confounder on day one.
contradictions.fix: Distinguish between outlets: 'Fortune reported none of the eleven limitations. Time, by contrast, carried the volume-confounder caveat on the day of publication, citing Osmani directly. The failure was not uniform across general-audience coverage.'

contradictions.quote: What we did find is that none of it crossed the boundary.
contradictions.counterexample: Time.com quoted Osmani's SMC comment on the volume confounder and Tucker on automation bias not being unique to AI, on the day of publication. ASCO Post quoted the authors' own acknowledgement of the observational limitation and Mori's caveat about prior RCTs. Both are non-specialist outlets that carried substantive caveats.
contradictions.fix: Replace 'none of it crossed the boundary' with a more precise claim: 'The volume confounder and the observational design did cross the boundary in some outlets — notably Time and ASCO Post — but the eleven limitations as a body, the Polish screening-programme suspension as the specific mechanism, and the call for randomised crossover trials did not appear in general-audience coverage.'

contradictions.quote: Its headline put the same result a different way: doctors became 20% worse at spotting abnormalities on their own.
contradictions.counterexample: Medscape, writing for clinicians, also reported both the 20% relative and 6% absolute reduction in the same sentence without choosing between them, and additionally reported the AI-assisted ADR (25.3%) for comparison — a figure Fortune omitted. The dual-framing problem Fortune exemplifies is real, but it is not universal even in non-specialist medical coverage.
contradictions.fix: Note that Medscape preserved both framings in the same sentence, making Fortune's headline-only relative framing a specific editorial choice rather than a universal pattern.

contradictions.quote: Three named academics said so publicly the day it appeared. Almost none of that survived the trip out of gastroenterology.
contradictions.counterexample: Time.com quoted two of the three SMC academics (Osmani and Tucker) on the day of publication, carrying their specific caveats about workload and automation bias to a general readership. 'Almost none' is an overstatement; the most important single confounder (volume doubling) did survive in at least one major general outlet.
contradictions.fix: Revise to: 'Three named academics said so publicly the day it appeared. The volume confounder reached at least one general outlet (Time) via those comments. What did not travel was the full body of eleven limitations, the specific mechanism of the Polish screening suspension, and the call for randomised crossover trials.'

contradictions.quote: The paper carries a published correction of 10 September 2025 [referring to Gerlich]
contradictions.counterexample: PubMed records a correction to the Budzyń colonoscopy paper itself, published November 2025 (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025 Nov;10(11):e12, epub September 11 2025). The draft does not mention this correction to its primary study anywhere in the text or sources, though it tracks corrections carefully for other papers.
contradictions.fix: Add to the Budzyń source entry: 'A correction to this paper was published in Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol November 2025 (10(11):e12). The nature and scope of that correction should be verified and disclosed.'

coverage.what_this_piece_can_add: No outlet found — including the careful specialist ones — reported the specific mechanism behind the volume doubling (the Polish national screening-programme suspension on 1 January 2022 freeing capacity to draw from waiting lists), nor did any general-audience piece report the confidence interval, the absence of withdrawal-time data, or the exclusion of the first 100 procedures per centre as a named limitation. The draft's unique contribution is therefore not the existence of caveats — those did travel, partially — but the precise causal account of why the population plausibly changed, and the demonstration that even the 2026 scoping review that assembles this literature for doctors mislabels the study design in its own abstract and miscites the Savardi paper: failures of transmission that occurred inside the specialty, not just at its boundary.
